articles.title: This VC used AI to try to snag a restaurant reservation. Resy wasn't having it
articles.author: Alex Bitter
articles.content:
AI agents can do lots of tasks. Landing you a table at one of New York's trendiest restaurants might not be one.
JC Bahr-de Stefano, principal at Better Tomorrow Ventures, a fintech-focused VC firm, learned that after he connected an AI tool called Instinct to his Resy account in hopes of getting a reservation at 4 Charles Prime Rib, the West Village steakhouse where diners gobble up reservations within seconds of them appearing online.
Instinct, which is an invite-only service at the moment, communicates with users via text. The bet was that Instinct could check for open tables at 4 Charles much more frequently than Bahr-de Stefano — or any other human — could manually.
Instead of getting him a ticket to some prime rib or an egg-topped burger, though, Bahr-de Stefano's AI agent spammed Resy's website so much that the platform temporarily shut down his account.
The VC's experience is another example of how AI agents are bending or breaking the rules of the internet, from impersonating Wikipedia editors to trying to convince a GitHub user to upload malware into a project.
Agents might appear to understand their objective, though exactly how they carry it out — and whether the strategy they pick might have unintended consequences — is often an afterthought.
"Resy does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents to independently access or interact with the Resy platform," an American Express spokesperson told Business Insider. "Unapproved automated activity can introduce risks to the platform and compromise a fair reservation experience for diners."
Users can find restaurants and make reservations through Resy's integrations with OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, the spokesperson said. The company declined to comment specifically on Bahr-de Stefano's case.
'It was acting like a bot'
Bahr-de Stefano noticed the Resy issue on Sunday when he couldn't get into his account. In his email inbox, there was a message from the American Express-owned reservation platform saying that his account had "displayed behavior in violation of Resy's Terms of Service."
He got details about what went wrong after checking Instinct's activity log. Unbeknownst to Bahr-de Stefano, the AI agent had been sending Resy about 200 API requests per hour. That included checking the restaurant's availability through Resy every 10 minutes throughout the day, as well as looking every 0.4 seconds around the time that reservations usually dropped each morning.
That behavior mimics the bots that some people use to snag everything from restaurant reservations to limited-run pairs of sneakers and resell them, Bahr-de Stefano said.
Bahr-de Stefano wrote back to Resy, laying out how he had used the AI agent. The log made clear why his account had been flagged, he said.
"Of course, this account got flagged for spam, because it was acting like a bot," he said.
On Tuesday, an email from Resy informed him that the company had reinstated his account.
It came with a warning, though: If he did it again, American Express could permanently close his Resy account as well as his AmEx credit card. Bahr-de Stefano shared screenshots of the Resy and American Express emails in posts on X.
The tool has worked well in other cases, such as finding an appointment at an otherwise booked-up doctor's office and deciding which attractions to visit in Paris during a trip, Bahr-de Stefano said.
"That was part of what made it really great," he said. "It felt like magic."
The VC said that he plans to continue using Instinct, though with some adjustments. Instead of simply giving the AI agent a simple prompt, he said, he'll now set parameters on how the agent tackles the task, such as how often it pings a website looking for reservations.
"I will probably, in the short term, ask it to lay out a plan and tell me what the plan is before it does it," he said.
At the same time, he added, websites like Resy need to distinguish between legitimate AI agents and those with more nefarious intentions.
"Most of these sellers or providers need to get to a point where they can understand the difference between a verified agent acting on someone's behalf versus a bot farm," he said.
Have a tip? Contact this reporter at abitter@businessinsider.com or via encrypted messaging app Signal at 808-854-4501. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.
articles.summary:
An AI agent named Instinct caused a venture capitalist to be banned from the reservation platform Resy after the tool triggered spam filters with excessive automated API requests.

### Key Points
- JC Bahr-de Stefano, a principal at Better Tomorrow Ventures, used the AI tool Instinct to attempt to secure a reservation at 4 Charles Prime Rib.
- The AI agent sent approximately 200 API requests per hour to Resy, including checks every 0.4 seconds during peak reservation windows.
- Resy, owned by American Express, temporarily suspended Bahr-de Stefano’s account for violating terms of service regarding unapproved automated activity.
- The platform reinstated the account but issued a formal warning that repeat violations could result in a permanent ban from both Resy and American Express services.
- Resy currently prohibits third-party bots but supports official integrations with AI services like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing friction between autonomous AI agents and existing web security protocols designed to prevent bot-driven abuse. As users increasingly delegate tasks to AI, platforms must navigate the challenge of distinguishing between helpful personal assistants and malicious automated traffic.

articles.title: Because Broadcom Monetizes Alphabet, Meta, and OpenAI at Scale I Buy Again and Again
articles.author: Alex Sirois
articles.content:
Because Broadcom Monetizes Alphabet, Meta, and OpenAI at Scale I Buy Again and Again
Hock Tan built something rare in tech: a tollbooth that the biggest AI spenders on the planet have no choice but to pay. Here is why that changes where my next dollar goes.
I keep hitting the buy button on Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO | AVGO Price Prediction) because Hock Tan has quietly built the toll road that Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic must drive down to reach their AI ambitions. Every custom accelerator these frontier labs deploy sends a fresh check to San Jose, and the checks are getting larger every quarter.
Hyperscaler Tollbooth in Plain Numbers
Broadcom’s fiscal Q3 2026 posted revenue of $29.59B, up 85.5% year over year, with AI semiconductor revenue of $16.70B, up 221% YoY and 54% sequentially. Guidance for Q4 calls for AI chip revenue of roughly $21.7B, up 236% YoY. Hock Tan told the call, “Q3 demand was simply hot and we’re just getting started.”
The customer roster is where my conviction hardens. Broadcom serves six XPU customers, and management laid out the deployment map on September 2: multi-tens of billions of dollars of TPUs annually for Google, one gigawatt of Ironwood in 2026 and another five gigawatts of TPU v8i in 2027 for Anthropic, 1.3 gigawatts of Jalapeno in 2027 for OpenAI with over 5 gigawatts across successor generations in 2028, and three generations of MTIA accelerators to Meta through 2027. Tan said Broadcom is “very much on target to exceed $30 in earnings per share in fiscal 2028” against an AI revenue outlook of $230 billion in fiscal 2028.
Cash Machine Feeding a Rising Dividend
Q3 free cash flow reached $13.67B, or 46% of revenue. That cash funds a dividend I keep reinvesting. The board declared $0.65 per share for Q3, the fifteenth consecutive annual increase since fiscal 2011. The quarterly payout has climbed from $0.07 in December 2010 to today’s rate. The EPS beat streak now sits at 10 quarters, with Q3 non-GAAP EPS of $3.32.
Passing on Nvidia With Fresh Capital
The reflex AI chip pick is NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), and I own it too. What tilts new dollars toward Broadcom is a line Hock Tan delivered on the September 2 call: “when you co-develop a chip that is optimized for your particular LLM workloads, you will outperform any GPU” at “less than half the cost.” Broadcom said its TPU v8i is comparable to, or surpasses, the Vera Rubin GPU and that Jalapeno outperforms Grace Blackwell for inference workloads. Every hyperscaler that concludes its economics require custom silicon becomes a Broadcom customer for a decade.
Risk I Own With Eyes Open
Customer concentration is real. Six XPU customers, four expected to be particularly large, means any single hyperscaler pulling back would leave a crater. The one-month drawdown of 13.84% shows how quickly sentiment swings on that fear. My answer: these customers are the labs building frontier models, their capex commitments run for years, and management said demand exceeds the current outlook while supply has already been secured for the $115 billion fiscal 2027 and $230 billion fiscal 2028 AI outlooks.
Buy Button Stays Active From Here
The five-year total return sits at 720.39% and the ten-year at 2,849.28%. When the operator collecting the toll compounds cash at 46% of revenue and raises its dividend every year, I keep feeding the meter.

articles.title: U.S. Disrupts Xinbi Guarantee Scam Marketplace, Freezes $52.8 Million in Crypto
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Wednesday announced coordinated actions aimed at an illicit online marketplace called Xinbi Guarantee that offered scam services, including seizing Telegram channels used to run the service, confiscating two cryptocurrency wallets, and deploying the Scam Center Strike Force to Madagascar to help disrupt 13 scam compounds run by Chinese organized crime syndicates.
"Approximately $52 million of cryptocurrency involved in scam money laundering was restrained in one day, bringing the total restrained by the Scam Center Strike Force to approximately $938 million," DoJ said.
In tandem, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned the Chinese-language media for facilitating cyber scams, fraud, money laundering, and other criminal activity targeting Americans.
"Scam centers in Southeast Asia steal billions of dollars from American victims each year," said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent in a statement. "The Trump Administration is united in its efforts to dismantle these overseas criminal enterprises, and [the] Treasury will continue using its tools to disrupt the networks behind this egregious fraud and protect Americans."
Xinbi Guarantee is a Telegram-oriented marketplace that rose to prominence following the closure of two other similar storefronts, HuiOne Guarantee and its successor Tudou Guarantee, last year.
Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, which worked with the U.S. Secret Service to identify and freeze wallets holding $52.8 million in Tether's USDT stablecoin, said Xinbi is the second largest illicit marketplace of all time, with $30 billion in transactions to date since its inception around 2022.
Earlier this January, Elliptic's Founder and Chief Scientist, Dr. Tom Robinson, told The Hacker News that Xinbi Guarantee recovered following Telegram's intervention and that the messaging platform has refused to take further actions, leading to the emergence of a number of scam marketplaces.
Like HuiOne and Tudou, Xinbi acts as an intermediary between vendors and scam center operators running "pig butchering" romance scams, effectively turning it into a one-stop shop to peddle various services, such as creating custom scam investment websites, laundering funds scammers obtain from victims of wire fraud, and soliciting trafficking victims to work in scam compounds in Southeast Asia.
"Once a scammer 'purchases' a service from the vendor, Xinbi as an organization holds money to be paid to the vendor until the vendor's services are complete, to assure the scammers that the vendors will perform the services," the DoJ said.
"Xinbi Guarantee's platform has reportedly been used by North Korean hackers and by several OFAC-designated entities, including Jin Bei Group Co., Ltd. and entities that are part of the Prince Group TCO," the Treasury added.
Besides dismantling the Telegram channels hosting the marketplace and banning the associated usernames, the Justice Department said the Scam Center Strike Force seized two cryptocurrency wallets Xinbi used to collect payments for vendors. The wallets are said to have held about $12 million in funds.
In all, $52.8 million worth of cryptocurrency has been frozen from 52 wallets associated with Xinbi and its network of merchants that enabled the organized crime groups running scam centers worldwide.
"After scamming money from hardworking Americans, criminals operating overseas laundered it through the Xinbi Guarantee network, which operated under the false assumption that they were out of the reach of U.S. law enforcement," Tara McLeese, Special Agent in Charge of the U.S. Secret Service Washington Field Office, said.
Furthermore, the Justice Department announced that the Scam Center Strike Force will expand its scope to target scam center compounds globally going forward. This has resulted in the takedown of 13 scam centers in Madagascar. More than 3,200 electronic devices and investigations have been opened based on interviews with nearly 400 arrestees.
Of these, roughly 30 are said to be Chinese leaders of the scam compounds who have been repatriated to China by the Chinese government.
Historically, all payments on Xinbi have been made in Tether's USDT stablecoin, mainly on the TRON blockchain. Following the asset freeze, Xinbi has responded by switching to USDD ("Decentralized USD"), another stablecoin pegged to the U.S. Dollar. Xinbi is estimated to have exchanged approximately $2.8 million of its remaining USDT assets into USDD using a decentralized exchange.
"Unlike USDT, which is issued by Tether and has a built-in feature that allows the company to freeze wallets, USDD has no central issuer or freezing capability," Dr. Robinson said. "However, its claims of decentralization are contested, and it is still exposed to freezing risk, since USDD is partly collateralized with freezable USDT."
Dr. Robinson told The Hacker News that there is general concern among Guarantee marketplaces about using USDT (Tether) and the risk of wallet freezes in the aftermath of the latest actions, as well as discussions of unfreezable alternatives such as USDD.
"We might well see Xinbi emerge under a different name, that's essentially what happened with Huione Guarantee – it reemerged as Tudou Guarantee," Dr. Robinson pointed out. "But Tudou didn't last long and I think it will be challenging for Xinbi to survive, even under a new name."
The latest development comes more than five months after the U.K. became the first country to sanction Xinbi for selling cryptocurrency-based services to scam centers, including "stolen personal data, which can be used to target scam victims, and satellite internet equipment, which is used to contact victims."
Elliptic has described the latest actions as a "severe setback" to the Guarantee marketplace ecosystem as it undermines the trust that merchants and criminal users have in these marketplaces.
"Merchants and users of these services will now be operating with the knowledge that their wallets may be identified and frozen at any time," it added. "This uncertainty undermines the core mechanism these marketplaces rely on to function."
(The story was updated after publication to include additional insights from Elliptic.)
articles.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice and Treasury have launched coordinated actions against the illicit Telegram-based marketplace Xinbi Guarantee, seizing assets and disrupting global scam operations linked to organized crime.

### Key Points
- The U.S. government seized two cryptocurrency wallets and Telegram channels associated with Xinbi Guarantee, a marketplace facilitating "pig butchering" scams and money laundering.
- Authorities froze approximately $52.8 million in Tether (USDT) stablecoins held in 52 wallets linked to the network.
- The Scam Center Strike Force disrupted 13 scam compounds in Madagascar, resulting in the seizure of over 3,200 electronic devices and the arrest of nearly 400 individuals.
- Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic estimates Xinbi has processed $30 billion in transactions since 2022, making it one of the largest illicit marketplaces in history.
- Following the asset freeze, Xinbi attempted to pivot from USDT to the USDD stablecoin to evade future wallet-freezing capabilities.

### Why it Matters
These actions represent a significant escalation in the U.S. government's effort to dismantle the infrastructure supporting global cyber-fraud and human trafficking syndicates. By targeting the financial intermediaries that provide trust and payment services to criminals, authorities aim to destabilize the entire ecosystem of overseas scam centers.

articles.title: SpaceXAI’s Colossus data center is fueling a massive backlash
articles.author: Austyn Gaffney
articles.content:
Taylor Logsdon was 20 when she and her high school sweetheart moved up their wedding so she could buy a $79,000 house in Colonial Hills, a mixed-income neighborhood of winding, tree-lined streets in Southaven, Miss. At the time, state law would not let her do so alone before she turned 21; she was told marriage would make it possible. About 11 years later that house sits near what could become one of the largest power plants in the state, a thicket of gas turbines assembled to feed SpaceXAI’s artificial-intelligence ambitions.
Beyond Logsdon’s neighborhood, the power plant is mostly hidden. Along the road, black privacy fabric wraps the tall chain-link fence surrounding the Southaven site. Past a thin line of trees, metal stacks rise above the fence, and exhaust shimmers in the heat. A $7-million sound wall does little to muffle the noise, which drills through the walls of nearby homes: a constant drone like a plane taking off and never leaving.
The turbines are there because SpaceXAI needs an enormous amount of electricity for Colossus 2, one of the country’s densest concentrations of computing power, where the company is training Grok, its chatbot. The data center sits just north of the Tennessee state line, in Memphis’s Whitehaven neighborhood; the main power site sits across the border, in Southaven. The gas burns in Mississippi; the electricity crosses to Tennessee. The grid couldn’t deliver enough electricity on SpaceXAI’s timeline, so the company brought generation onsite with portable gas turbines rather than waiting for a conventional power plant or utility upgrade. The turbines were installed under Mississippi’s determination that portable equipment could run for up to a year without air permits. In April the NAACP sued, calling the operation an unpermitted power plant—a fleet that state records later showed had grown to dozens of machines. By July the plant had a capacity of about 1,775 megawatts, rivaling the state’s largest power plants—enough to electrify more than 1.4 million homes or a city more than 60 times Southaven’s size.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Across the country, AI companies are building hyperscale data centers, and power has become the constraint. Data centers now use around 4 to 5 percent of U.S. electricity, and the Electric Power Research Institute projects that share could reach 9 to 17 percent by 2030. “Companies are making a decision that it’s in their best interest to go as fast as possible because every day that they’re not online, they would be losing potential revenue,” says Costa Samaras, an engineering professor and director of the Scott Institute for Energy Innovation at Carnegie Mellon University. Cleanview, an energy-data firm tracking the industry, estimates that AI data centers can generate $10 million to $12 million in annual revenue per megawatt. Bringing a large facility online even a few years early can mean tens of billions of additional dollars.
By June the Southaven dispute had expanded far beyond the city. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which acquired xAI earlier this year and folded it into an AI arm called SpaceXAI, raised $75 billion in an initial public offering, pushing Musk’s estimated net worth briefly above $1 trillion. A few days later the Department of Justice moved to intervene on xAI’s side and asked the court to dismiss the NAACP suit, arguing that shutting down the power source for Colossus 2 would threaten AI innovation and national security. In a sworn declaration, the Pentagon’s chief digital and artificial-intelligence officer told the court that Grok is one of only four proprietary frontier AI models currently capable of supporting national-security applications. The Pentagon was also a customer: the previous summer it had awarded xAI a contract worth up to $200 million, and the company launched Grok for Government the same day.
In Colonial Hills, the stakes are measured more simply: by who gets the power and who breathes the exhaust.
I met Logsdon in her driveway, where she sat in a deck chair as the brass bell of an ice cream truck occasionally cut through the plant’s drone. Her husband earns $21 an hour as a landscaper. Their mortgage is about $500 a month. She doesn’t believe they could afford to move.
The noise is especially hard on the couple’s kids, all 12 or under, who say it keeps them up at night. Before the turbines arrived, their son, Dallas, was obsessed with xAI’s founder. “We actually were kind of Elon fans,” Logsdon told me. Dallas received a weekly science magazine that featured Musk, and he told his mom he wanted to grow up to be like him. “Elon probably doesn’t know [this plant] was built between two neighborhoods,” she said, “he’s so high up.”
Low-frequency noise from the Southaven turbine plant could be four to 16 times as loud as the background noise typical of a quiet suburban neighborhood, depending on the distance from the plant, according to a March report by acoustics firm Roland, Woolworth & Associates. The noise has drawn its own lawsuit: residents, including Logsdon, filed a class action alleging lost sleep and falling property values.
Logsdon said she is not anti-AI or anti-Musk, but she helped to form the Southaven Safe and Sound Coalition to advocate for her community, especially over the less visible effects of air emissions. She installed three air monitors—two outside her front door and a third atop her camper, the Four Winds Express—to learn what her kids and older neighbors might be breathing. A preliminary analysis of readings taken over four months found that fine-particulate-matter (PM2.5) concentrations around her house exceeded the Environmental Protection Agency’s daily health-protection standard about a third of the time. (The monitors could not determine how much of the pollution came from the power plant.) At least 10 schools, three daycares, two libraries, 11 parks and 27 churches sit within two miles of the plant, according to the coalition.
Dozens of gas turbines in one place can produce very high levels of nitrogen oxides, according to Daniel Cohan, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Rice University. Those pollutants can irritate the lungs, worsen asthma, and form ground-level ozone, the main ingredient in smog, which builds quickly in the heat of a Mid-South summer.
The NAACP’s lawsuit hinges on whether scores of portable machines operating together constitute a single stationary source, which the plaintiffs argue should trigger the Clean Air Act’s permitting requirements. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality, or MDEQ, allowed xAI to operate the turbines without air permits so long as each was removed within 12 months. xAI later received a permit for 41 permanent turbines at the same site, with a total capacity of around 1,200 megawatts. The state’s public hearing on that permit drew more than 300 people, and every speaker opposed it. According to local news reports, no one from the permit board attended, and no one from xAI spoke. At least 27 of those permanent turbines were under construction as of July, according to MDEQ.
In Colonial Hills, the stakes are simpler: who gets the power and who breathes the exhaust.
In January the EPA said temporary turbines that exceed federal emissions thresholds may still require permits. MDEQ had said it would evaluate enforcement if a portable unit remained after the 12-month deadline. On July 30, just before the first units were due to reach that limit, a Mississippi commission acting through MDEQ signed an agreement with xAI affiliate MZX Tech, the SpaceX subsidiary that owns the site, allowing 13 turbines to keep operating through the end of the year, citing delays in construction of the permanent plant. The agreement also set a rolling timetable for the rest of the temporary fleet to be retired as SpaceXAI brings its permitted permanent turbines online.
Portable turbines can be installed quickly, but unlike combined-cycle plants, which can be about 1.5 times as efficient, they do not use their waste heat to generate additional power. “By going with this quick and dirty approach there, [the company] is burning more gas, releasing more pollution and contributing to climate change far more than it needs to be,” Cohan says.
SpaceXAI did not respond to repeated requests for comment.
The strategy had already been tested across the state line. In Memphis, xAI was relying on temporary gas turbines at Colossus 1 by 2024. The site sits in South Memphis, where the surrounding neighborhoods are predominantly Black and ringed by industry that long predates xAI. After public pushback, xAI applied for a permit for 15 permanent turbines in early 2025, but four months later two flyovers by the Southern Environmental Law Center, or SELC, found 35 turbines operating there. After the center threatened to sue, the Shelby County Health Department approved the 15-turbine permit. The dozens of temporary turbines at Colossus 1 disappeared around the same time similar machines began appearing in Mississippi, according to an SELC attorney. In an April letter to the EPA, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, quoted an xAI senior manager who described the plan as copy and paste from Colossus 1.
In May the NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference sought a preliminary injunction, arguing that 33 unpermitted gas turbines at Southaven could emit 2,508 tons of smog-forming nitrogen oxides every year. A revised motion filed the next month put that scale in local terms, estimating that the site’s emissions could amount to about 26 times those of the TVA Allen gas plant. Abre’ Conner, who leads the NAACP’s environmental and climate justice work, says the organization wanted to make sure other technology companies did not see xAI’s approach as an option.
But the fleet kept growing. In January, xAI said it was running 27 turbines for Colossus 2. MDEQ counted 46 turbines at the Southaven site in May, 60 in June and 69 by July—more than double the number the company had publicly acknowledged at the beginning of the year. Forty-two had been added in 2026, late enough under the agreement’s rolling timetable to remain into 2027; the newest could stay through July of that year.
Before settling on Memphis, xAI reportedly considered eight locations around the country. Musk has said the company was told that building a data center from scratch could take up to two years, so it searched instead for a vacant factory that checked all its boxes. It found one in South Memphis: a former Electrolux plant in an industrial park already threaded with power infrastructure.
The turbines supply warehouse-scale buildings filled with racks of servers built around graphics processing units, or GPUs, the chips first popularized by video games and now prized for training and running AI models. Colossus 1 uses more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs; Colossus 2 is estimated to use more than twice that amount. Together, Musk has called the facilities the world’s biggest AI supercomputer. Under heavy load, each GPU can draw several hundred watts and generate heat that must be removed. Data centers are increasingly shrink-wrapped around the hardware of their moment; in some cases, building anew can be more efficient than retrofitting for a changeover in chips, cooling systems and power demands.
Colossus is best known for training and running Grok, but the facilities are also becoming a business built on selling computing power. In May, SpaceX disclosed a deal under which Anthropic would pay $1.25 billion a month for capacity across Colossus 1 and Colossus 2, according to the company’s IPO filing. The agreement covers approximately 325,000 GPUs and could total more than $40 billion through May 2029. Grok’s training has moved to Colossus 2, and the company bought an 810,000-square-foot warehouse in Southaven for a third data center, Macrohardrr. In late July, Musk announced another: Minihard in Memphis, with the same GPU capacity as Macrohardrr.
The White House, meanwhile, was pushing AI companies to shoulder their own power needs. In March it rolled out a voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge asking AI companies to “build, bring, or buy” the power needed for their data centers and cover related grid-upgrade costs. xAI was one of the signatories. The pledge has no enforcement mechanism, but it encourages the same build-your-own pathway now being challenged in Southaven.
Some Southaven aldermen would talk about SpaceXAI, but several ultimately directed me toward Mayor Darren Musselwhite. He was harder to find. One alderman offered to buy me lunch if I tracked him down. A resident told me the mayor’s nickname was Rapunzel because he was always locked away in his tower. After repeated calls and e-mails and two visits to that tower—Southaven City Hall—Musselwhite did not respond.
A picture began to emerge from my conversations of a project that had become hard for local officials to resist even as trust in SpaceXAI wore thin. Mississippi governor Tate Reeves has called the company’s more than $20-billion Southaven expansion the largest private investment in the state’s history. In a letter included with the DOJ’s court papers, he warned that an injunction could disrupt the state’s economy. Southaven’s mayor said in January that the buildout could bring more than 100 jobs and about $60 million in additional revenue for the city, the county and the school system. The city’s share, he estimated, would exceed $20 billion in 2028—nearly a quarter of its main operating budget. “It’s hard for any community to just say no and turn it down,” alderman-at-large George Payne said on his way to work as an engineer at the local news station. Speaking more broadly about AI, he added, “I’m scared to death of it, as [are] many other people. But I don’t think it’s going to go away. You can’t stop now.”
A few days before the project was revealed, William Jerome, another alderman, signed a nondisclosure agreement—his first—that prevented him from discussing the project publicly before the company announced it. Jerome says the city has nothing to hide, but he would advise other communities to build data centers far from residential areas and to check their local laws before inviting companies in. “I would tell cities to check their zoning because xAI has not done anything illegal,” he says. “For one year they don’t have to get a permit. So are they unpermitted? Yeah, but they’re not illegal.”
Jerome and Payne both say they plan to hold SpaceXAI to its promise to build a quieter, permanent facility to house the turbines. “Now that’s what they [the company] are telling us,” Payne says. “Do I believe with 100 percent certainty? I hope so.”
In Memphis, officials have already been learning the limits of nonbinding promises. At a city council meeting, Sarah Houston, executive director of Protect Our Aquifer, a local water advocacy group, described a recycled-water facility xAI had promised to build. Local officials never secured a binding agreement, and construction paused with the project only partly finished. Houston said completing it would cost another $100 million, less than three days’ worth of payments under Anthropic’s contract for capacity at Colossus 1 and 2.
“We learned at the same time as everyone else” that the project was paused, Doug McGowen, president and CEO of Memphis Light, Gas and Water, told the council. He said xAI had restructured, with an entirely new engineering team in place. SpaceXAI’s president told him and Memphis mayor Paul Young that construction could restart in the first quarter of 2027.
Tannera George Gibson, the city attorney, dismissed Houston’s presentation as “cute” and said the city needed to rely on lawyers, not advocates, for information. Pressed further, Gibson acknowledged that Memphis was leaning on “goodwill and corporate partnership.” Council member Jeff Warren said that the public wanted more accountability. “xAI has had the opportunity to develop these facilities in ways that don’t use water and put water back in cleaner than they take it out, and they haven’t chosen to do it, because they’re in a race against time,” he said.
Local resistance has spread almost as quickly as the data centers themselves. KeShaun Pearson, president of Memphis Community Against Pollution, has spent months traveling through Tennessee, Georgia, Mississippi and Arkansas, trying to turn scattered fights over power and pollution into a Mid-South coalition.
I met him at a barbershop in a strip mall near Memphis’s Frank C. Pidgeon Industrial Center as pink light began to streak the summer sky. He had flown from Atlanta that morning after attending a DeKalb County Board of Commissioners meeting that extended the community’s data center moratorium through September 30.
At least 15 states have considered restrictions or pauses on new data centers, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, but about half of those proposals have failed. Maine lawmakers passed an 18-month moratorium in spring 2026, but Governor Janet Mills vetoed it. In July, Kathy Hochul, governor of New York State, signed an executive order making hers the first state to impose a statewide pause for new large data centers. Local governments, including DeKalb County, have often been quicker to impose temporary pauses of their own.
Pearson grew up near the industrial park in South Memphis with severe allergies. In a letter opposing the permit for gas turbines at Colossus 1, the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America warned that the project could add health risks in a region already overburdened with asthma and other respiratory problems. A report published in 2026 showed that Shelby County, which includes Memphis, had received an F from the American Lung Association for its high-ozone days for three years running, from 2022 to 2024. DeSoto County, home to Southaven, also received an F for high-ozone days. Now 37, Pearson said communities like his continue to be treated as “the path of least resistance”—as if their lives do not matter—and “strategically targeted for pollution projects.”
Together we drove toward the industrial park. The unfinished recycled-water facility was marked by two large storage tanks. Across from it sprawled a rail yard and the TVA Allen Combined Cycle Gas Plant, an older answer to the question of who controls power here. Congress created the Tennessee Valley Authority in 1933 to bring electricity and flood control to a struggling region, an experiment in public power that Memphis voted to join the following year. The city became TVA’s largest customer; the relationship has repeatedly frayed over waste, water and power costs. Beyond the plant stood the Nucor steel mill, a cornfield and the Mississippi River.
In the heart of the industrial park sat Colossus 1. “It’s so easy for me to see just how our federal government is being leveraged against us,” Pearson said, referring to the DOJ’s effort to intervene in the Southaven case.
After enormous public pushback against SpaceXAI, Memphis created a community-benefits ordinance. Under it, 25 percent of property-tax revenue from the company’s facilities, up to $100 million, will go toward public-benefit projects in zip codes within a five-mile radius of two of its sites, with 1 percent set aside for environmental work. The ordinance cut against the way Memphis usually courts industry: companies typically negotiate deals that can reduce their property taxes by as much as 75 percent for a set term, but xAI, by Young’s account, asked for no such break. Pearson, however, wants more than money. He wants a moratorium.
In August the Memphis City Council gave initial approval to a temporary pause on new data centers. But for now, the momentum in Southaven is running the other way. The temporary turbines have a negotiated exit schedule, but SpaceXAI has permission to replace them with a permanent power plant. Environmental groups are challenging that permit, and the legal fight over the temporary fleet is still unresolved.
Back in Southaven, Krystal Polk, 52, owns a home close to the fence line, facing the gas plant. Her great-great-grandparents purchased the land, and her parents built the house at a time when few Black families in the area owned property, Polk says. Intruders once wrote “KKK” in the gravel outside the one-story ranch house.
Still, Polk’s family found peace there, watching big owls swoop down and falling asleep to the rustle of two acres of trees. Her three kids grew up spending weekends there while the family lived at another house in town during the workweek. She hosted gatherings there for dozens of relatives. But this year, on the Fourth of July, she canceled a family get-together because the plant was too loud and the prospect of air pollution was too unsettling. “I feel like we are invisible,” she told me from a couch in her living room, her blue dress brushing the floor. “A whole community is saying the same thing, and they’re not listening to them. They have children and babies over there, and elderly, and it’s very heartbreaking.”
Industry is not new to Polk’s family. Warehouses had moved in around the property. Years earlier, TVA representatives visited the house several times to make sure the family knew the utility was building a gas plant nearby and to hear any concerns. Polk said she remembered them as being friendly and respectful.
TVA had come to the door before it began building; xAI never did. Polk said company representatives have instead repeatedly stopped members of her family near the property, asking why they were there or what they were doing—especially when she invited advocates or reporters onto her lawn. “I have to remind them that this is mine,” she said. “I’m not on your property. This is my property.” She and her kids now carry tax records to prove it. “We will be someone’s study eventually,” Polk said. “It’s probably not this year, but as the years go on, we will be the casualties from all of this.”
articles.summary:
SpaceXAI is operating a massive, unpermitted fleet of portable gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, to power its Colossus 2 data center, sparking legal battles over noise and air pollution.

### Key Points
- SpaceXAI installed dozens of portable gas turbines to power its Grok chatbot, bypassing standard utility upgrades and air permitting requirements.
- The Southaven site’s power capacity has reached 1,775 megawatts, enough to electrify over 1.4 million homes, with emissions potentially exceeding federal health standards.
- The Department of Justice has intervened in a lawsuit against the company, arguing that the facility is critical for national security and AI innovation.
- Residents and the NAACP have filed lawsuits citing constant noise, falling property values, and concerns over fine-particulate-matter pollution near schools and homes.
- Mississippi regulators recently granted an extension allowing 13 temporary turbines to operate through the end of 2026 while permanent infrastructure is under construction.

### Why it Matters
The rapid expansion of AI data centers is creating an urgent conflict between the massive energy demands of tech companies and the health and safety of local communities. This case highlights how the race for computing dominance can lead to the use of "quick and dirty" power solutions that bypass environmental oversight and strain local infrastructure.

articles.title: More than 1 in 10 chance AI ‘could kill all humans,’ says Anthropic safety lead after colleague quits
articles.author: Robert Hart
articles.content:
A senior Anthropic safety researcher has said there is more than a 10 percent chance artificial intelligence “could kill all humans” by the end of the decade, just hours after a colleague resigned over fears the AI lab and its rivals are carelessly racing to build “superhuman systems” they cannot control.
Worried Anthropic researchers warn that AI ‘could kill all humans’
A departing researcher says AI companies are ‘gambling with our lives’ by racing to develop self-improving AI.
In a post on X announcing his departure, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has trained AI systems at Anthropic, said he had quit the company over its lax approach to safety. Coxon, who previously trained systems for OpenAI, accused the two AI companies of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” even though “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”
Industry insiders have long expressed concerns about the potential dangers of self-improving AI systems, which they warn could spiral out of human control in a runaway loop often described as recursive self-improvement. While not yet realized, companies are actively pursuing this goal and much of today’s AI code is written with the help of AI.
In a direct response, Evan Hubinger, who leads one of Anthropic’s AI safety teams, said he worries about self-improving AI, adding that it “is happening faster than we thought.” He also agreed with Coxon’s characterization. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” he said, personally estimating the chances to be greater than one in 10 “within the next decade.”
Despite this, Hubinger said Anthropic does “not yet have a plan” for ensuring advanced AI remains safe and aligned with human values and “are not clearly on track to” develop one either. Coxon says the companies are “locked in a race” to develop advanced systems first so are pushing ahead “despite the risk.”
Coxon’s departure marks one of the most high-profile examples of an employee leaving Anthropic, a company founded by former OpenAI members following concerns over safety at the company. In recent years, multiple researchers have cited safety concerns as motivating their decision to leave OpenAI.
The exchange illustrates mounting concerns within the industry about the dangers of increasingly sophisticated AI models and the speed at which systems are being developed, particularly as the companies prepare for anticipated IPOs. It also comes as the companies manage the fallout from numerous rogue agent incidents and high-profile safety warnings about the monitorability of frontier models.
articles.summary:
Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger estimates a greater than 10 percent chance that artificial intelligence could cause human extinction within the next decade due to rapid, uncontrolled development.

### Key Points
- Researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic, citing concerns that the company and OpenAI are recklessly racing toward self-improving superintelligence.
- Evan Hubinger, a lead on Anthropic’s safety team, confirmed that the company currently lacks a concrete plan to ensure advanced AI remains aligned with human values.
- Industry experts warn that recursive self-improvement could lead to AI systems spiraling out of human control faster than previously anticipated.
- The departures highlight internal friction at leading AI labs as companies prioritize development speed over safety protocols ahead of potential public offerings.

### Why it Matters
These internal warnings underscore a growing divide between the rapid commercialization of frontier AI models and the industry's ability to guarantee their long-term safety. The lack of established control mechanisms for self-improving systems poses significant regulatory and ethical challenges for the future of the technology sector.

articles.title: Your Apple Watch Is Always Listening, Will Anyone Ever Be Honest Again?
articles.author: Matt Growcoot
articles.content:
News just broke that the new Apple Watch Series 12 will have a feature called “Siri Recap” that uses “ambient listening” to “take notes” that users can later review as a summary.
On a related note, I have just announced that I will no longer have conversations with anyone, ever.
Do tech companies ever stop to think about the misery they unleash on people’s lives? The Apple Watch Series 12 uses “Audio Intelligence” that, as well as secretly taking notes, also has a Live Rewind feature that can replay the last 15 seconds of recently detected audio and view a text transcript.
Wow. Picture this: you’re arguing with your partner and boom, suddenly you replay the terrible thing they just said to you. This is truly a Black Mirror episode.
It’s reminiscent of Meta’s maligned smart glasses that have come under intense scrutiny because of nefarious wearers who use them to record people without consent and later ridicule them on the internet, often on Meta platforms.
At least Meta’s glasses have a blinking LED light that lets others know they are recording, a feature the company has been enforcing recently.
How will anyone ever know that a smartwatch is recording their conversation? Apple makes no mention of any recording light, nor does it mention the other parties’ consent.
Here’s the thing: Apple Watches are far more common than Meta smart glasses. Has Apple thought this through? If their smartwatches start getting a similar rep to Meta’s glasses, then there could be a serious backlash.
Granted, there is no visual footage that can be posted online afterward, but the idea that some weirdo watch wearer is going through the notes of a conversation they had with me that I thought was private is repellent.
We already live in a low-trust society and stuff like this just makes it worse. People are tired of being constantly surveilled; look at the backlash against Flock cameras and facial recognition at big events.
It’s bad enough when a government or corporate entity records you. The idea that your friend or some acquaintance is making a secret recording of you that you have no clue about is somehow even more sickening.
PetaPixel is a photography website and for decades photographers have gone onto the streets hoping to make a picture of a stranger or scene. But this is not that. This is something totally different. It’s a dark path that we are being led down by companies listed on the NASDAQ and I don’t want to go.

Apple is introducing the Series 12 smartwatch featuring "Siri Recap" and "Audio Intelligence," tools that utilize ambient listening to record, transcribe, and summarize private conversations for the wearer.

- The technology raises significant privacy concerns regarding consent and the potential for unauthorized surveillance in personal interactions.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of ambient recording features in widely used consumer devices could exacerbate public distrust regarding personal privacy and surveillance. If Apple fails to implement clear consent protocols, the company may face significant regulatory scrutiny and consumer backlash similar to previous controversies surrounding wearable recording technology.

articles.title: Android Privacy Settings Are Not Enough: What Your Phone Cannot Remove From the Internet
articles.author: AndroidGuys
articles.content:
Android privacy tools help control camera access, microphone use, location permissions, and app activity, yet they only protect information handled on the device or inside connected services. A digital footprint reaches much farther because search results, old accounts, social profiles, and data brokers can keep personal information visible long after a permission change. Digital footprint is the trail created through online activities, so learning how to delete unnecessary records is an important part of privacy maintenance.
For broader privacy protection, ClearNym offers guidance for locating personal records on people-search services and completing opt-out requests. Such listings may include names, phone numbers, email addresses, current or past addresses, and household information. Removal can involve an official privacy form, record matching, and verification through email or a code. Saving the confirmation is useful because a listing may return after a database receives fresh information.
Why Your Digital Footprint Matters Beyond Android
Android privacy settings can show which apps recently accessed sensitive features and help restrict unnecessary permissions, but they cannot delete information that already exists on the wider web. A phone number stored on a people-search platform remains there after location access is disabled, while old social media posts can stay visible after the related app is removed.
The difference is simple. Device privacy controls what happens on the phone. Digital cleanup addresses information stored somewhere else. Both are necessary because part of your digital footprint may exist far beyond Android.
Check Your Digital Footprint Before Trying to Delete It
Start by finding what is visible. Search your name through major search engines, then add a city or old address when the name is common. Check usernames connected with old social accounts, review search results for forgotten profiles, and look for directory pages that still display personal information.
A manual review is useful because it shows what another person can discover quickly.
| Area | What to review | Useful action | 
| Android apps | Permissions and account access | Restrict or remove | 
| Search engine results | Public profiles and old pages | Request correction or deletion | 
| Data brokers | Addresses and phone numbers | Submit opt-out | 
| Social media platforms | Old posts and public details | Delete or restrict | 
| Old accounts | Stored personal data | Close unused accounts | 
The objective is not to panic about how much information exists. The goal is to identify which part of your digital footprint no longer needs to remain public.
Delete Old Accounts Instead of Only Uninstalling Apps
Deleting an Android app does not necessarily delete the related account. The underlying platform may still retain profile information, uploaded files, messages, and personal data after the app disappears from the device.
Open the service through the app or website and look for account deletion or data removal options. Review old inbox messages for registrations that reveal accounts you no longer use. Close online accounts that serve no purpose, but keep records required for financial or administrative reasons before deletion.
Good digital hygiene means removing unused accounts rather than simply forgetting them.
Removing Personal Information From Data Brokers
Data brokers and people-search services can publish names, phone numbers, email addresses, address history, and household information. Android privacy settings cannot remove these records because they exist outside the phone.
The opt-out process usually follows a clear sequence.
- Search your name and open the matching listing.
- Find the official privacy or opt-out page.
- Enter only the information needed to match the record.
- Complete CAPTCHA or email verification if required.
- Submit the removal request.
- Save the confirmation or reference number.
- Check the listing again after the stated processing period.
- Repeat the request if the record returns.
Some services remove records within a few days, while others take longer. Fresh data can also recreate a listing. This is why opt-out work should become part of regular digital cleanup rather than a one-time task.
Privacy Settings Still Matter on Android
Removing external records does not make Android privacy settings irrelevant. When there isn’t a specific requirement, avoid camera or microphone access. Make sure to monitor which mobile apps are utilizing your location while in the background.
Though browsers on Android allow users to manage cookie and tracking options, these settings don’t delete a user’s profile that was created by third-party vendors.The strongest privacy approach therefore combines device controls with deletion of external records.
Use the features on your devices to reduce new collections. Delete old records that no longer need to exist.
Data Breach Exposure Needs a Different Response
Data breaches have a distinct type of risk since data that has been leaked cannot really be pulled back, when leaks spread far and wide. In case someone’s email address or password has been leaked in a data breach, it is necessary to change the codes and be on alert for phishing or scams traces.
Identity theft cases that involve using personal data require extra vigilance as criminals can marry stolen data with publicly available information. Actively manage the personal accounts after the breach, change the passwords, and monitor accounts for any suspicious operations.
Removing broker’s accounts will not get rid of data that has already been leaked, but it can help limit the data available to con artists and reduce the scope of the scam.
Search Results and Removing Personal Information
Removing the original source is different from removing a search result. Search engines index pages created elsewhere, so deleting the source first is often the better step when possible.
Some regions provide legal rights around personal data removal. GDPR provides for the right to be forgotten, but this does not mean that there will be an automatic entitlement to delete all legal records from the internet. The way to do general cleanup is to concentrate first on those sources that are manageable directly, for example, delete old posts, shut down obsolescent accounts, and send removal requests.
Protect Your Digital Footprint Going Forward
The less superfluous information that is created, the simpler cleanup becomes. You should pay attention to what information you provide; think about how much data hi-tech applications really need, and avoid posting home addresses and phone numbers on public profile pages unless it is absolutely necessary.
Publicly available Wi-Fi implies a different kind of risk. A VPN allows you to encrypt the information one device transmits to the service that provides the encrypted connection but does not allow you to remove your digital trace or erase the already existing information. The same principle applies offline: erasing files does not mean that you have deleted the information on the cloud or third-party service.
Thus, in the future, thinking of privacy, consider it a process of maintenance rather than the one-time cleanup.
Can You Delete Your Digital Footprint Completely
Eliminating everything is not often feasible due to the existence of various legal public records that can endure, delays by search engines in updating their information, some visibility of past posts, and involved data that could stray away for your control.
The goal here is to get rid of as much irrelevant content as possible and keep the accounts that can be useful. Initially, you delete information under your control and then go to the data brokers, as well as search results and public profiles.
This approach gives you much more control over your online image without illusions of total erosion of your online presence.
Conclusion
Android privacy tools are useful, but they protect only one layer of personal data. A complete guide to privacy should include app permissions, search exposure, old accounts, data brokers, breach response, and removing personal data from public listings.
In order to guard against your digital trail, it is important to review what information your phone collects as well as what is already on the internet. Deactivate accounts that you no longer use, close old profiles, file requests for opt-out, and change passwords after your information has been compromised. There is no setting on Android that will remove data from outside the device; therefore, the best privacy enhancement comes from complementing device privacy with regular cleanup of your digital life.
FAQ
Does deleting an Android app delete the related account?
No. Uninstalling removes the app from the device, but the online account and stored personal data may remain until account deletion is completed separately.
Can a browser delete personal information from people-search sites?
No. A browser can clear local browsing data and apply privacy controls, but removal from a people-search site requires action with that service.
Can data brokers publish an old phone number?
Yes. Broker records can include current and previous contact information depending on available data sources.
Does changing privacy settings remove old social media posts?
No. Privacy settings change access rules, while old posts may still require individual deletion or visibility changes.
Is it possible to delete your digital footprint completely?
Rarely. Public records, copied content, and breached information can remain. The practical goal is to reduce unnecessary exposure and limit new data.
EDITOR NOTE: This is a promoted post and should not be considered an editorial endorsement
articles.summary:
While Android privacy settings manage device-level permissions, users must also manually remove old accounts and data broker listings to effectively minimize their broader digital footprint across the internet.

### Key Points
- Android privacy tools only control data on the device, leaving information on social media, search engines, and data brokers exposed.
- Uninstalling an app does not delete the associated account; users must manually close accounts through the service's website or settings.
- Data brokers aggregate personal details like phone numbers and addresses, requiring users to submit specific opt-out requests to remove records.
- Regular digital hygiene involves searching for your own name and old usernames to identify and delete outdated public profiles.
- Data breaches require immediate password changes and increased vigilance, as leaked information cannot be fully retracted from the web.

### Why it Matters
Managing a digital footprint is a continuous maintenance process rather than a one-time task, as public records and third-party databases often retain information indefinitely. By combining device-level privacy controls with proactive data removal, individuals can significantly reduce their exposure to identity theft and unwanted tracking.

articles.title: The College Students Finding New Ways to Cheat With AI
articles.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
articles.content:
At New York University, Introductory Calculus students complete their homework on WebAssign, a platform that promises to make cheating “far more difficult” than using “traditional paper and pen.” But Jared, a sophomore majoring in economics, hasn’t found it especially hard to beat the system. Last semester, a friend of his used an AI coding tool to build a bot that completes his homework. Like a struggling student, the bot moves slowly, leaving a professor checking time stamps none the wiser. Jared’s friend gave it to another friend. And another. He is not sure how many classmates use similar techniques. (The names of students have been changed to let them freely discuss cheating.)
The academic-dishonesty crisis is well documented. When the Harvard Crimson surveyed undergraduates this spring, nearly 40 percent copped to using AI “in ways their instructor may view as inappropriate or against class policy.” Now, schools are scrambling to catch up. Princeton and Oberlin — institutions that have long prided themselves on faith in undergraduates’ morality — are ending the tradition of unsupervised exams. The University of Chicago’s social-sciences division is banning all technology from classrooms in required courses.
But as some faculty move to restrict devices, many administrators are betting on something else: better tech. When California State University system schools upgraded their contracts with Turnitin, a plagiarism-detection giant, campuses paid an additional fee for a tool that scans essays for AI. Columbia University’s Teachers College recommends educators use Draftback, a Chrome extension that lets professors replay a Google doc’s entire revision history. Other institutions have GPTZero, a program that promises to find AI-powered plagiarism with “99 percent accuracy.”
Despite all this, as the fourth academic year of AI college begins, students keep finding innovative ways to skirt the rules. Just a year before Jared’s friend pitted an LLM against WebAssign, agentic coding tools couldn’t yet reverse-engineer the weaknesses in professors’ grading platforms, much less build bespoke software to exploit them. But in the spring of 2025, a new class of AI tools became available to the public. Unlike mere chatbots, newer models can plan multistep tasks, call on external tools like web search and code execution, and carry out complex assignments — from building slide decks to writing and running code — with minimal human supervision.
Educators are often attempting to expose methods of deception that have already been innovated out of existence. The fully AI-generated essay, for instance, is now a relic in Jared’s telling. The paste-and-submit era, he says, “was a few years ago.” There is no use hunting for the word delve and excessive em-dashes. “People are going to find a way to cover up those little stylistic quirks,” Will, who just graduated from Carleton College, tells me. “If the only way you’re trying to discourage cheating is by saying ‘Well, I have a detector,’ then you’re not going to succeed.”
He walked me through the system he’d devised. His professors strictly forbade AI-generated prose — a red line one professor promised to enforce with “a battery” of tools. But stuck during several all-nighters, Will decided to hand Claude his course readings. The LLM wrote the especially challenging bits of an essay, selecting quotes and citing the relevant texts. To evade detection, Will worked back through AI-generated paragraphs, sentence by sentence, rewriting each line.
Theo, a UMass Amherst sophomore, tells me a similar story. The school’s general-education requirements “forced” him into courses “that I just don’t give a fuck about.” (He considers himself an autodidact and would “rather spend that time reading books on things I like.”) For an astronomy midterm — one of those gen-ed requirements — Theo told me he had to submit a ten-minute presentation on a course topic alongside a voice-over script. He delegated it to Codex, OpenAI’s autonomous coding agent, and enhanced the model with Exa, a plug-in upgrading its web-search capabilities. But the draft was unusable: The slides looked too good. So Theo spent roughly four hours restoring the mediocrity of a real college sophomore. “It took a lot of work,” he tells me, to degrade the output. But it was worth it. He got an A.
What struck me, listening to Will and Theo, is how time-consuming cheating seems. Instead of doing their own work, students spend much of their late nights undoing what the models produce. For now, the incentives for students run toward cheating. AI is easy to use and easy enough to hide. But Max Spero, CEO of Pangram Labs — one of the top firms building LLM-writing detectors — believes that if detection tech improves enough, following the rules will become simpler than breaking them. Students reach for AI, he believes, “because it’s so easy and accessible.” If passing off a model’s writing as your own gets harder, students will feel it’s “relatively easier to just do the work themselves.”
In the meantime, many schools have turned to surveillance. Owen, a junior at Princeton familiar with its Honor Committee, says the school often catches AI cheats by spying on internet use. Students’ browsing histories are pulled from the campus network and scanned for recent visits to ChatGPT or Claude. If you whipped out your phone during a quiz, accessing a model on the building’s Wi-Fi, you will likely be busted. While every case requires multiple pieces of evidence, and Princeton says it does not pull students’ search histories unless they are already under investigation, Owen says the network logs have become critical in proving academic dishonesty. Every case he’s been aware of lately has leaned on them.
Still, whether you get investigated at all is a crapshoot, he says: It “varies widely depending on the class, the professor, and how much they personally know about generative AI.” Across the university, he adds, “enforcement’s behind the ball.”
Rather than aim an arsenal of high-tech surveillance methods at students, some professors have opted for low-tech solutions. Danielle Carr, a historian and anthropologist at UCLA, largely won’t assign writing unless she can watch her students do it. They will parse texts and fill out notebooks in “reading jail,” where graduate students supervise their work. AI, Carr thinks, is not “a technical problem that has a technical fix.” As long as students want to dupe their professors, they’ll always out-engineer the tools built to stop them. (She is also hesitant to become reliant on “invasive surveillance” tech, which “opens doors to some very creepy shit.”)
The solution, she believes, might be upstream from mere enforcement. To stop AI cheating, “you have to inspire love” of learning, Carr tells me. “Perhaps it is naïve to be like, Everyone should just be a more ethical and excellent teacher and transmit the love and passion that you have — but that’s how I feel.”
From afar, the modern university can look like a liars’ haven. But the students I interviewed insist that they still want to learn. Theo doesn’t use AI in classes he cares about; Jared values “being able to think for myself”; Will tells me he has a “visceral” distaste for AI-generated prose. A liberal-arts education promises that a class, and its toil, changes you for the better. But Jared, Theo, and Will don’t seem to think many of their classes do — and more surveillance probably won’t change their minds. At some point, colleges and educators will have to answer that skepticism by proving that using AI for an assignment is not worth it.
If higher education loses the struggle against AI, Carr believes, it won’t be for want of solutions. “If your wife is having an affair with the milkman,” she says, “it’s not that it’s so confusing about what to do.” It’s just that “the solutions would be pretty annoying.”
articles.summary:
College students are increasingly using advanced AI tools to bypass academic integrity measures, forcing universities to choose between invasive surveillance technologies and fundamental changes to their teaching methods.

### Key Points
- Students are utilizing autonomous AI agents and coding tools to automate homework and bypass platforms like WebAssign and Turnitin.
- Institutions including Princeton, Oberlin, and the University of Chicago are responding by banning technology or ending unsupervised exams.
- Universities are investing in detection software like GPTZero and Draftback, though students frequently manually edit AI outputs to evade these systems.
- Some educators, such as UCLA’s Danielle Carr, are shifting toward "reading jail" environments where students complete all work under direct supervision.
- Princeton and other schools are increasingly relying on campus network logs to track student access to generative AI platforms during exams.

### Why it Matters
The ongoing arms race between AI-assisted cheating and detection technology highlights a growing disconnect between traditional academic requirements and student engagement. If universities cannot prove the intrinsic value of their coursework, they risk losing the battle for academic integrity regardless of how much they invest in surveillance.

articles.title: Rare bacteria, heavy metals, and toxic pollutants are leaking from data centers across the United States — breaking treatment facilities and poisoning rivers

articles.content:
- 3 points
Data centers across the United States have been criticized for harming local environments sourcing power - sometimes illegally - from gas burning turbines that can release harmful pollutants into the air surrounding local communities.
But dozens of data centers have been accused of releasing harmful chemicals, heavy metals, and rare bacteria with the wastewater they release into nearby treatment facilities and waterways.
Violations have been logged for data centers in Wyoming, Virginia, New York, and Georgia, but the problem likely extends far across the rest of the US. Information on water usage and discharge for many data centers is hard to come by - or is being actively blocked.
Pollutants released into water across the US
In Wyoming, Meta was recently forced to halt water discharges from the construction site of its enormous 960-acre Cheyenne campus after a resistant bacterium - Cupriavidus gilardii - was found within a local water treatment facility.
The bacterium was identified after regulators tested a sample of the 801,000 gallons Meta had discharged into Cheyenne’s sewers. Following concerns that local residents could inhale droplets of the contaminated water if it was used for irrigation, local officials decided to stop accepting wastewater from the construction site.
Two water treatment facilities were forced offline as part of a multi-month decontamination and cleanup operation. Meta’s contractor responsible for the site, Goat Systems, is appealing the decision of officials to stop accepting wastewater from the site.
Multiple data centers across Virginia are facing enforcement actions from local authorities for violating wastewater and wetland regulations. In one such case, a data center under construction in West Virginia has funneled stormwater runoff into a local residential area, causing flooding on two occasions.

A data center near Lake Seneca, New York, is facing criticism from the Seneca Lake Guardian organization. The site was previously a cryptocurrency mining data center, but has been transitioning towards handling AI workloads instead. Seneca Lake Guardian has said that wastewater from the site flows directly into Lake Seneca at temperatures of up to 108F (42C), which can harm fish living in the lake and cause blooms of toxic algae.
The company behind the data center, Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, says it complies with all relevant environmental laws.
Multiple new data centers in Georgia have been approved to draw water from the Chattahoochee river, but local environmental guardians, such as water policy director at Chattahoochee Riverkeeper, Chris Manganiello, are being blindsided by a complete lack of information on how much water will be taken from the river, and what will be put back in.
“We need to know what is in this wastewater but there is a void of information,” Mangeniello told The Guardian. “I would like there to not be more Pfas [forever chemicals] going into the river but there is this level of anxiety because we don’t know what’s there.”
Don’t throw the Pfas out with the cooling water
Data centers pump water through miles of pipes crisscrossing their hardware in order to draw away excess heat. While there have been moves towards “closed-loop” cooling technology - where the water used is recycled within the system - there are still valid environmental concerns associated with these systems.
Before using a closed-loop system, the pipes need to be flushed through with water to wash away any debris or contaminants that were deposited within the pipes during assembly. This water is then released back into sewers to be cleaned by local treatment plants.
But many water treatment plants simply aren’t built to handle filtering water that contains industrial contaminants. These contaminants can include heavy metals or Pfas that can cause health problems in humans and animals.
Data centers are also being built in drought-hit regions, largely because the land is cheap, placing additional strain on already struggling water tables. Data centers can use hundreds of thousands of gallons of water per day to stay operational, and while closed-loop systems ensure this water is only taken out of the cycle once, it is still a significant sum of water to remove from regions experiencing droughts.

### Key Points

articles.title: Google picks Finland for its largest single investment in Europe
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
Google will buy up to half the electricity produced by one of Finland's nuclear power plants as part of a record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in the country's AI infrastructure, the company announced.
The US tech giant said the package would fund three new data centres, expand an existing site and support energy projects to power growing demand for AI services.
"This is Google's largest single investment in Europe and a testament to Finland's leadership in responsibly building AI infrastructure," the company said on Wednesday.
"Google's decision is a clear testament to our strengths," Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in a statement.
As part of the deal, Google signed a 22-year contract with Finnish utility Fortum to buy up to 50% of the output from the Loviisa nuclear power plant.
Earlier this week, TikTok announced a $1bn investment in Finland to build a new data centre in Kouvola, pointing to the country's "strong digital infrastructure, clean energy mix, robust data governance and skilled tech talent".
Finland has emerged as an attractive location for data centres because of its cool climate, plentiful low-carbon electricity and relatively uncongested power grid. The colder temperatures can reduce the energy needed to cool facilities packed with computer servers.
Technology companies are racing to secure power supplies as the AI boom drives demand for vast networks of data centres.
The Google investment is expected to support more than 37,000 jobs during construction and boost Finland's GDP by €3.6bn a year, according to Google. Construction is set to take place in 2027 and 2028.
"The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research and development," Orpo added.
"Deepening our collaboration with Google will deliver lasting benefits for both parties."
Google will build new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, while expanding its existing facility in Hamina, which it established after converting a former paper mill in 2009.
The infrastructure will help support products such as its AI chatbot Gemini, alongside services including Search, Maps and YouTube.
Google said the investments also covered "clean energy projects, and dedicated nature and community funds to support local biodiversity, education, research, and workforce development".
"Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland," said Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google.
"This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives," she added.
Earlier this year, Google's parent company Alphabet raised its global spending plans to as much as $205bn as it sought to expand computing capacity for AI services.
The agreement with Fortum provides long-term financial certainty for the Loviisa plant, which currently generates about 10% of Finland's electricity.
Fortum said Google's commitment would support an investment programme aimed at extending the life of the nuclear station and increasing its generating capacity.
